items.why_watch: Rather than just debunking flat earth claims, this video uses them as a springboard to stress-test real physics — asking what the evidence actually requires us to believe and why. It's a clever pedagogical move: working through a wrong model rigorously often clarifies why the right model works. At 32 minutes it earns its runtime by going deeper than the usual dismissals.

Does light (photon) experience time? The most common answer to this is, no. Light does not experience time. But, that's not accurate. So, in this video, let's explore what physics really has to say about this

00:44 Visualising time dilation

items.why_watch: The standard answer — 'light doesn't experience time' — turns out to be a lazy shorthand, and this video carefully unpacks why that framing breaks down under scrutiny. The creator uses spacetime intervals and the geometry of light's worldline to show what physics actually says, making this a good corrective for anyone who picked up the oversimplification from a pop-science source.

items.title: Demystifying The Metric Tensor in General Relativity
items.description:
The path to understanding General Relativity starts at the Metric Tensor. But this mathematical tool is so deeply entrenched in esoteric symbolism and complex mathematics that its simplistic, intuitive purpose often goes neglected. Here we attempt to expose the basic principles behind the Metric Tensor -- and investigate how they tie into General Relativity -- in as simplistic a manner as possible. Do we succeed? Feel free to let us know in the comments!

Support us on Patreon! https://www.patre
items.why_watch: The metric tensor is the gateway concept to General Relativity, but most treatments either drown you in index notation or stay so vague the math never connects to meaning. This video prioritizes the intuition first — what does the metric tensor actually measure and why does curved spacetime need it — making it a genuinely useful entry point before tackling a textbook.

themes.name: Silicon Brains, Real Fast
themes.tagline: How computers think faster than you can blink — no fluff, just elegant hardware logic.

items.title: Binary adder - Carry Select Adder
items.description:
This video is about the Carry Select Adder. It is an adder used in microprocessor when you want to sacrifice area to get an advantage in speed.

Carry Skip Adder: https://youtu.be/WmIFFhJYzO0

Binary Operations: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLnAxReCloSeTrpY-9q7ECY8ju8Fpi1mzP
items.why_watch: Carry Select Adders are a classic speed-vs-area tradeoff in processor design, and this short video gets straight to the mechanism without padding. If you've ever wondered how hardware arithmetic gets optimized beyond the obvious ripple-carry approach, this is a clean, efficient explainer to bookmark.

morning_soundtrack.title: Garth Brooks’ 2026 “Blame It All On My Roots” Tour: How to Get Tickets
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The tour finds Brooks reviving his in-the-round Drum Pod stage and performing multi-night stands at arenas around the country. Garth Brooks’ 2026 “Blame It All On My Roots” Tour: How to Get Tickets Paolo Ragusa
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The smell of sawdust and stadium beer, 20,000 strangers singing every word like it's a hymn they were born knowing.

global_silver_linings.title: Rural French Mayors Rally to Save Their Local Cafe-Bistro, and Help Reverse National Trend
global_silver_linings.snippet: With the help of the mayor and local council, a small town in Burgundy has saved its local cafe-bistro, what’s been described as the “heart” of the rural French economy and society. Au Bon Accueil, located in the commune of Saint-Martin-sur-Ouanne, had closed recently for 8 months, giving a nasty shock to locals who realized […]
global_silver_linings.reason: When local leaders band together to save a village café, they're protecting far more than a place to eat — they're preserving the communal heartbeat of rural life. It's a reminder that communities can push back against decline when people choose connection over convenience.

global_silver_linings.title: Winners of Bird Photographer of the Year announced
global_silver_linings.snippet: The winners of Bird Photographer of the Year 2026 have been revealed
global_silver_linings.reason: The Bird Photographer of the Year competition brings the world's most extraordinary avian moments into sharp focus, rekindling wonder at the biodiversity still thriving around us. Every winning image is quiet proof that there are people devoted to witnessing and honoring the natural world.

global_silver_linings.title: Crayola has retired just 13 colors in 123 years. The first 8 led to protests.
global_silver_linings.snippet: Don't mess with people's childhoods, man.
global_silver_linings.reason: The fact that people cared enough about crayon colors to stage protests is a charming testament to how deeply small, creative joys become woven into childhood and memory. It's a lighthearted reminder that ordinary things can carry extraordinary meaning.

global_silver_linings.title: From fire starters to compost: what to do with dryer lint
global_silver_linings.snippet: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If you clean your dryer’s lint trap after every load, you end up with a soft little cloud of fiber in your hand pretty regularly. Most people drop it straight in the trash, and that is fair. But if you get in the habit of saving it in a […] The post From fire starters to compost: what to do with dryer lint first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .
global_silver_linings.reason: Dryer lint turning out to be genuinely useful — as a fire starter or compost additive — is the kind of small, satisfying discovery that makes sustainable living feel approachable rather than overwhelming. Waste that was already in your home becoming a resource is a quiet win worth celebrating.

discovery_articles.title: Benedictine Monastery Holy Trinity of Las Condes in Las Condes, Chile
discovery_articles.snippet: A beautifully designed modern church and monastery of the 1960s. The site has been considered a link from city to the mountains. Walking up the main driveway gradually exposes the Andes before revealing the church.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The architects didn't just build a church — they choreographed a pilgrimage, engineering the driveway so the Andes reveal themselves incrementally as you walk. It's sacred theater disguised as a parking approach.

discovery_articles.title: A Rare Aztec Codex Detailing the Rise and Fall of Tenochtitlan Returns to Mexico for the First Time in Nearly Two Centuries
discovery_articles.snippet: The artifact, among the most prized visual accounts of Aztec history, will be on display in Mexico City for three months
discovery_articles.ferns_note: This codex watched Tenochtitlan rise to glory and then collapse under conquest — and then spent nearly two centuries in European hands before coming home. Some objects carry grief the way wood carries rings.

discovery_articles.title: Did Thomas Jefferson Father Sally Hemings' Children? After More Than a Decade of Research, the Answer Is Finally Firmly in Hand
discovery_articles.snippet: A lock of hair, advances in genetic science and a community of descendants all contributed to solving an American mystery
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A single lock of hair, kept for over two hundred years, became the final thread in untangling one of American history's most charged and long-denied secrets. The dead, it turns out, are remarkably patient witnesses.

discovery_articles.title: A Cutting-Edge English Initiative Replaces Lawnmowers With Scythes to Restore Wildflowers and Save the Bees
discovery_articles.snippet: English Heritage has recruited volunteers to mow meadows the old-fashioned way at some of its historic sites
discovery_articles.ferns_note: English Heritage is handing volunteers scythes — actual scythes — not as a heritage stunt, but because the old blade disturbs the soil less and lets wildflower seeds survive where a mower would mulch them into silence. Sometimes the ancient tool simply wins.

discovery_articles.title: The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, a New Endeavor From the Creator of 'Star Wars,' Is a Story in Itself
discovery_articles.snippet: Almost two decades in the making, the institution centers on art that shapes our everyday lives and reveals the craft behind it
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Nearly twenty years of false starts, city fights, and redesigns before a single visitor walked through the door — George Lucas's museum is itself the kind of underdog narrative his films are famous for telling. Life imitating art, rather literally.

discovery_articles.title: France Celebrates the Bicentennial of Photography with Traveling Themed Exhibitions
discovery_articles.snippet: In our era of digital screens and virtually endless images and videos, it's a challenge to imagine the time before photography existed.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Two hundred years ago, a person could live an entire life and never once see their own face accurately rendered — photography didn't just change art, it changed the very human experience of being seen. That's worth pausing on, even mid-scroll.

featured_read.title: What Were My Dreams Trying to Tell Me?
featured_read.snippet: To make sense of my deepest experiences, I needed a new way of talking about the soul.
featured_read.blurb: When the language of psychology felt too clinical and religion felt too inherited, one writer went looking for a third vocabulary — one honest enough to hold what dreams actually do to us. A quiet reckoning with the parts of inner life that resist easy naming.

reading_room.title: He was probably right
reading_room.snippet: Cicero’s life and thought are a testament to the idea of probabilia: we should be confident in our beliefs, but never certain - by Massimo Pigliucci Read on Aeon
reading_room.blurb: Cicero never claimed to know the truth — only to pursue the most probable version of it — and Massimo Pigliucci argues that two thousand years later, that intellectual humility is still the most rigorous stance available to us. A bracing corrective to our era's twin vices of certainty and cynicism.

reading_room.title: 50 Years Ago, NASA Unveiled its First Space Shuttle
reading_room.blurb: The story of how a coordinated letter-writing campaign by "Star Trek" fans strong-armed NASA into naming its first shuttle Enterprise is a delightful footnote about the moment popular culture realized it had actual political weight. Small history, enormous charm.

reading_room.title: Lesser choices
reading_room.snippet: Estelle recalls being blindfolded and fearful in Mexico City – a timely vision of a world without abortion rights - Directed by Courtney Stephens Watch on Psyche
reading_room.blurb: Through one woman's blindfolded memory of a clandestine procedure in Mexico City, this short film asks what it means to navigate your own body in a world that has decided it knows better. Spare, visceral, and impossible to dismiss.

reading_room.title: On “Derek,” Captain Ahab’s Evil Half Brother
reading_room.snippet: “Your worst enemy ain’t Moby Dick, it’s your half brother, Derek.”
reading_room.blurb: What if Ahab's obsession isn't unique — what if it's actually a family trait, and somewhere out there Derek is also ruining perfectly good whaling expeditions for entirely petty reasons? A genuinely funny meditation on literary villainy and the absurdity of the heroic grudge.

reading_room.title: Tomato Cure
reading_room.snippet: "The quiet medicine of small jobs, finished before dark."
reading_room.blurb: There is a particular kind of healing that only arrives through repetitive, low-stakes physical work — weeding, harvesting, washing — and this essay follows a summer of tomatoes as a grief that couldn't be spoken is slowly, wordlessly composted. Set aside the full half-hour; you'll want to sit with the ending.

garden_note.note: Zürich wakes this equinox morning with a certain golden-hour gravity — the year pivots on its heel today, and the garden knows it, leaves just beginning to bronze at their tips while the dahlias and late asters hold their colour with admirable stubbornness.
in_season: Asters (Herbstastern) opening in violet and rose
Harvesting winter squash and pumpkins before the first frost
Planting garlic cloves and spring bulbs while the soil is still warm
garden_note.sky_tonight: The waxing gibbous moon rises early and floods the garden with silver light by nightfall — look also for Saturn, well-placed in the southeast after dark.
garden_note.sun_times: First light arrives at 06:42, with sunrise at 07:11 — and on this equinox the sun sets at 19:25, dusk lingering until 19:54.

news.title: My Easy Trick for Making Roasted Broccoli Taste Ridiculously Good
news.snippet: I make this version of roasted broccoli pretty much every week because it’s just that good. Florets get roasted on a preheated baking sheet until browned and caramelized. Then they’re buried under buttery panko and sharp cheddar and broiled until golden-brown and crisp.
news.blurb: A clever weeknight trick that turns humble broccoli into something caramelised and genuinely crave-worthy — worth a read if you've ever sighed at a sad sheet pan of greens.

news.title: Sumac roast chicken and bread bake: Sami Tamimi’s fattet musakhan with cucumber avocado salad – recipe
news.snippet: A rich Levantine fusion dish of sumac-spiced roast chicken, onion and flatbread with tahini yoghurt, and a simple, textured salad Fattet musakhan , a celebration of two beloved Palestinian dishes, takes centre stage here, bringing together crisp bread, creamy yoghurt, sumac-spiced onions, tender chicken and fragrant olive oil in one rich and comforting dish. Alongside, the salad brings a welcome freshness, with crisp cucumber, creamy avocado and bright acidity cutting through the richness of the chicken. Together, they make a beautifully balanced meal, bringing the generous, communal spirit of Palestinian cooking to the table.
news.blurb: Sami Tamimi's fattet musakhan is a gorgeous love letter to Palestinian cooking, and the sumac-roasted chicken alone is reason enough to bookmark this one immediately.

recipe.title: Pie Recipes: Favorite Sweet & Savory Pies
recipe.snippet: A collection of my most loved pie recipes, the ones I can't stop baking. Sweet or savory, fruit-filled or hand-held, these pies come out of the oven beautiful and fragrant. Classic at heart, with just enough modern edge.
recipe.blurb: Whether you're in the mood for something fruit-filled and sweet or warmly savoury, this beloved collection of classic pies — beautiful and fragrant straight from the oven — is exactly the kind of baking project a cosy afternoon was made for.

larder.seasonal_note: Zürich's markets are heady with Berner Rosen and Gravensteiner apples right now — pick up a kilo from the Bürkliplatz stalls and slow-cook them into a chunky Apfelmus scented with a little cinnamon and lemon zest, the kind that makes the whole kitchen smell like a sensible kind of happiness.

fern_data.greeting: Crayola has retired just 13 colors in 123 years — and the first eight cuts caused actual protests. That small, stubborn fact belongs in the same edition as an Aztec codex returning to Mexico after nearly two centuries away.
